extracted.intended_audience: architects, designers, ornament-makers, and students of architectural aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for where, how, and when to use ornament in architecture and related decorative arts, emphasizing legibility, fitness to purpose, proportion, and abstraction. Focuses on avoiding false or misplaced decoration and on principles that make ornament truly architectural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inscriptions: place and legibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Place inscriptions where they will be read, and there only; write them plainly — 'Write it as you would speak it, simply; and do not draw the eye to it when it would fain rest elsewhere.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat inscriptions as architectural or pictorial ornaments. Make them plainly written, not turned upside down or wrong end first. Avoid decorative flourishes on lettering ("do not put a dash and a tail to every letter"); the inscription's only merit is its sense, so sacrifice nothing of legibility to beauty. Use plain tablets for necessary writing rather than ornamental scrolls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ribands/scrolls as ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Never use ribands/flying scrolls as ornamental forms — they have 'no structure... no skeleton, no make, no form' and are 'vile' and spoiling to nearby work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ribands are a succession of cut threads all alike: they cannot assume true graceful form or wave with natural strength. Do not introduce scrolls for the sake of the scroll; if writing needs a support, use a tablet, not a flourished scroll used as ornament. Historical authority (Raphael, Ghiberti) does not justify their routine use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drapery only as exponent of motion or gravitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Drapery is noble only insofar as it expresses motion or gravitation; 'all noble draperies... are the exponents of motion and of gravitation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat drapery as an ornamental subject by itself. When used properly it indicates past/present motion or the force of gravity; Christian sculptors used heavy falling drapery to express repose, Greeks to express movement. Drapery used for its own sake (e.g., merely decorative folds) is base.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place natural ornament where nature would place it
rubrics_metrics.description: When borrowing objects of nature for architecture, place them in such associations and positions 'as may befit and express their origin' — i.e., where Nature would have placed them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carve leaves, flowers, festoons, etc., so they appear rooted or connected (as the Corinthian capital 'looks as if the leaves had one root, though that root is unseen'). Avoid tacking exuberant flowerwork in unnatural positions (e.g., a heavy bunch tied across a blank wall) where it becomes an 'ugly excrescence'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid festoons/garlands in unnatural contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Garlands and festoons are appropriate where their natural function makes sense (a garland belongs on a head), not hung on walls or used as mismatched circular ornaments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a round ornament is needed, use a flat marble circle, star, or medallion rather than carving a garland that looks used and withered. Do not display garlands as if they were hung up to dry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use trivial or ill-fitting decorative excrescences (e.g., dripstone handles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Small, incongruous decorative additions (like a dripstone shaped as a drawer-handle over a square-headed window) are offensive: they break unity and appear 'glued' on without support or harmony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect the character of the principal form (e.g., the square as an exponent of power). If you cut or break its terminal lines with added ornament you lose unity; avoid fragmentary, isolated lines that have no relationship to structure or decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not decorate objects of active use or business
rubrics_metrics.description: A general law: 'Wherever you can rest, there decorate; where rest is forbidden, so is beauty.' Do not mix ornament with tools, workplaces, or things belonging to active life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ornamenting mills, millstones, ploughs, ledgers, or shop fittings that serve business functions. Ornament presented amid active use will either be ineffective or will vulgarise the object and the ornament itself. Reserve decoration for places and objects of repose (drawing-rooms, domestic furniture) where people can contemplate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-sensitive shop and street decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: Shop decoration only makes sense when the shop is part of a dwelling and lived in; modern separated shop fronts should not carry temple or palace ornament gratuitously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In medieval contexts, upper stories and the dwelling received richest decoration; in modern cities, gratuitous Greek mouldings and friezes over shops are valueless and vulgarise the forms themselves. If shops and houses are inseparable, decorate the whole house consistently; otherwise remove shop ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ornamenting railroad stations and transit places
rubrics_metrics.description: Railroad stations are places of hurry and discomfort; ornament there is 'mere mockery' — the architect's duty is safety and speed, not beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not spend on ornamental columns, patterns, or costly decoration for stations; invest in solid materials, strong carriages, good servants and workmanship. Keep ornamental work out of the way of functional transport buildings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not disguise necessities with decorative masks
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid hiding functional necessities (e.g., ventilators in flat roofs) behind ornament; this associates beautiful forms with ugly or unsuitable contexts and diminishes their pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even well-designed ornament, when constantly used to conceal ugly necessities, becomes dishonored and loses its pleasurable influence (examples: roof roses concealing ventilators which are never appreciated by congregations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament must be imitative and hierarchically chosen
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Ornamental' is that which is imitative: the nobler the thing imitated, the nobler the ornament — 'imitated flowers are nobler than imitated stones... imitated human form... the noblest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine forms (rock, fountain, river, plants, animals, human figure, angel) appropriately; choose subjects of imitation by their inherent order and dignity to achieve noblest ornamental effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place ornament where it can be intellectually perceived
rubrics_metrics.description: Architectural imitation represents what can be perceived by deliberate examination; ornament demands an intellectual exertion similar to that by which Nature's forms are understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not present subtle imitative forms where the viewer cannot focus or engage (busy workplaces, hurry contexts). Over-presenting beautiful forms when the mind cannot attend will deaden and 'defile' them; repetition in wrong times/places destroys their meaning and pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the eye vs ear: be careful presenting visual expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The eye... cannot choose but see.' The eye is less easily numbed than the ear; therefore visual expressions presented at inappropriate times or places will more readily weary and debase the form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid violently attaching lovely forms to vulgar objects or in incongruous situations; the eye will be filled and weary, and the form will be associated with vulgarity. Present visual ornament where the viewer's mind can respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural qualities: Proportion and Abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: The two essential conditions for architectural ornament are Proportion and Abstraction: architecture delights in abstraction and prominently exhibits calculation of parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proportion in architecture is not a fixed set of ratios but a compositional necessity. Abstraction means selecting a few characteristics out of many rather than completing forms fully (architecture 'fears to complete her forms'). Both distinguish architectural ornament from pictorial or purely sculptural ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion rule: a dominant member is required
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever Proportion exists at all, one member of the composition must be either larger than, or in some way supreme over, the rest — 'There is no proportion between equal things.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symmetry of equal things yields agreeableness but not composition; to compose is to arrange unequal things. Use inequality (a supreme element) to achieve proportion and avoid mere symmetry which lacks compositional hierarchy.
